newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovakia cautioned over EU membership.
newsitem.headline: Slovakia cautioned over EU membership.

text.p: Slovakia, increasingly unlikely to be among the first wave of new NATO members, was warned on Wednesday that it also risked missing the train of integration into the European Union.

European parliamentarian Herbert Boesch said at the end of a three-day meeting of a joint EU-Slovak parliamentary committee that a botched referendum in May had further weakened Slovakia's chances of being among leading contenders for EU admission.
"The train (towards EU enlargement) is already moving and we have stressed that it depends on Slovakia alone if it is to be able to catch up with it," Boesch said.

Slovakia wants to be among the first new members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) and EU but its chances of making the first wave for NATO have waned after repeated Western criticism of its pace of democratic reform.

"There is no sense in our being officially assured of Slovakia's firm determination to become a member of the EU when we also have the feeling that in day-to-day policy various politicians and institutions are placing obstacles before this aim," Boesch said.

Two referendums last month, on NATO membership and on direct elections of the president, ended in chaotic failure after the government refused to include the election question on the ballot, on the basis of a controversial legal interpretation.

The referendum on elections was called by the opposition in an attempt to stop Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar taking on presidential powers when incumbent President Michal Kovac's term in office ends in March.

Under the present system, parliament elects the president. But in the current deeply-split assembly, no candidate would gain the required three-fifths majority. In that case, presidential powers would temporarily pass to the premier.

Boesch said rectifying the impasse between government and opposition had been one of three points of a recommendation on improvements to the political climate and culture in Slovakia which would send a positive political signal to Brussels.

The other two recommendations were on enabling access of opposition parties to parliamentary committees overseeing the secret service and military intelligence, and passing a law on the use of minority languages in official communications.
The three matters had been the subject of previous concern on the part of the European Parliament which has so far been ignored by the ruling coalition.
Augustin Marian Huska, co-chairman of the joint commission and deputy chairman of the Slovak parliament, said both sides had agreed that the three points must be implemented by next November.

"These are the prerequisites for a signal of the will of Slovakia towards integration," Huska said, adding that the joint commission had positively assessed Slovakia's progress in economic and social affairs.
